summary.title: Machine learning force field ranking of candidate solid electrolyte interphase structures in Li-ion batteries
summary.authors: James M Stevenson; Garvit Agarwal; Leif D Jacobson
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses the critical challenge of simulating the Solid-Electrolyte Interphase (SEI) in lithium-ion batteries, a complex system where existing Density Functional Theory (DFT) methods fail due to computational cost or accuracy limitations. The authors propose a novel workflow combining a multitask Quantum-Reference Neural Network (QRNN) machine learning force field (MLFF) with advanced sampling techniques, including Artificial Force Induced Reactions (AFIR) and Nudged Elastic Band (NEB). By training the model on a diverse dataset encompassing general organic chemistry (SPICE) and specific battery components, they successfully generated and ranked candidate SEI structures. The model was validated against high-level wB97X-D3BJ DFT calculations for reaction barriers and surface energies. Results indicate that P-F and Li-O bonds correlate with higher stability, while C-O and Li-F bonds correlate with lower stability. This work provides the first quantitative ranking of SEI candidate structures, offering a pathway for future experimental validation and material optimization, despite limitations in the current single-electrolyte formulation scope.

Executive Summary
This study addresses the critical challenge of simulating the Solid-Electrolyte Interphase (SEI) in lithium-ion batteries, a complex system where existing Density Functional Theory (DFT) methods fail due to computational cost or accuracy limitations. The authors propose a novel workflow combining a multitask Quantum-Reference Neural Network (QRNN) machine learning force field (MLFF) with advanced sampling techniques, including Artificial Force Induced Reactions (AFIR) and Nudged Elastic Band (NEB). By training the model on a diverse dataset encompassing general organic chemistry (SPICE) and specific battery components, they successfully generated and ranked candidate SEI structures. The model was validated against high-level wB97X-D3BJ DFT calculations for reaction barriers and surface energies. Results indicate that P-F and Li-O bonds correlate with higher stability, while C-O and Li-F bonds correlate with lower stability. This work provides the first quantitative ranking of SEI candidate structures, offering a pathway for future experimental validation and material optimization, despite limitations in the current single-electrolyte formulation scope.

Research Context
The SEI is vital but poorly understood, combining organic and inorganic components. Key questions about SEIs, such as whether they are amorphous or crystalline, remain unanswered. Existing pure density functionals work well for metallic systems but tend to badly underestimate reaction barriers. Even these fastest of the useful density functional theory (DFT) methods are much too slow to study the time and length scales of the SEI. Hybrid functionals such as wB97X that yield improved barrier heights struggle with metals. MLFFs promise to allow atomistic simulation with the accuracy and wide applicability of DFT.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can a multitask MLFF model accurately predict SEI energetics and reaction barriers? Does multitask learning with general organic chemistry data improve model capacity without overfitting? Can enhanced sampling methods like AFIR and NEB generate plausible SEI candidate structures? Do specific bond types (e.g., P-F vs C-O) correlate with SEI structural stability? Is the QRNN architecture stable enough to simulate extreme conditions relevant to SEI formation?

Methodological Details
The study used a combination of classical sampling and a novel machine learning model. Reference levels included wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD for non-periodic and PBE-D3 for periodic systems. We used the multitask abilities of QRNN to add a totally distinct dataset of general organic chemistry. We used the SPICE subset consisting of elements H, Li, C, O, F, and P. We added our own GFN1-xTB atomic partial charge labels to the SPICE data. We generated initial SEI candidate structures using a method newly released in the Schrodinger suite. Each system starts with 700 molecules of EC and 52 ions each of Li+ and PF 6 -. This gives a 1 M solution with 7416 total atoms. We defined four sets of candidates with different levels of added Li: 5, 12, 23, and 33. We then annealed them using our reactive QRNN model with NPT MD at 400 K and 1000 atm. We ranked each set of candidates by calculating the mean potential energy of each structure.

Procedures And Architectures
We used a combination of classical sampling and a novel machine learning model. Our loss function is the same as that used in previous QRNN works, consisting of energy and atomic force mean squared error. Because of the addition of the SPICE dataset, we had four output levels of theory in total. We used the Adamax optimizer with decoupled weight decay. For our final model we used a learning rate of 2e-3. We used hidden layers of size 256, 224, and 192 for all elements. We found that a high level of weight decay, 3e-3 per batch, was helpful. For our final model we used a more conventional weight decay of 1e-3. We performed periodic DFT using Quantum Espresso as implemented in Schrodinger Materials Science Suite. The exchangecorrelation energy was determined using generalized gradient approximation (GGA) Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) functional. We performed gas-phase wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD DFT using Psi4 v1.6. We focused on a relatively small part of reactive chemical space, the known decomposition reactions of EC.

Key Results
We produced the first set of SEI candidate structures ranked by predicted energy. We validated our model against the best available calculations for surface reaction energy barriers. We observed no increase in PBE-head validation RMSE on the battery datasets when adding the SPICE data. We observed only an 8% increase in hybrid-head RMSE when adding the SPICE data. P-F and Li-O bonds are associated with more stable structures. C-O and Li-F bonds are associated with less stable ones. Our QRNN models gave stable dynamics despite the extreme conditions applied. The list of SEI candidate structures and energies can be found in the provided repository.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
This work demonstrates that multitask training with a QRNN model allows an MLFF to model complex SEI reactions. This is the most complex redox reactive system simulated using an MLFF or any method of comparable accuracy. The latent space of these MLFF models contains unused capacity that can be applied to broadening chemical applicability. Future work should include the application of other model architectures, including Nequip and MACE. MLFFs offer a powerful opportunity to understand SEI materials, but only if we are willing to tolerate working in an environment where theoretical and experimental references are currently limited.

Contradictions And Limitations
The difficulty of characterizing the SEI system experimentally is a strong motivation for this work, but also an obstacle to validation. We cannot compare the density, diffusivity, viscosity, or elastic modulus of our SEI material against experimental values. We have so far constructed SEI candidates using only a single formulation of electrolyte, 1M LiPF 6 in EC. We do not regard our current model as final, since its scope is still small compared to what is required. The probability of being proven wrong by future events is high.

Claims
Multitask training with general organic chemistry data improves MLFF capacity without significant performance loss on battery tasks. We observed no increase in PBE-head validation RMSE on the battery datasets. We observed only an 8% increase in hybrid-head RMSE. This result is significant because it means the latent space contains unused capacity. Unlike the addition of reaction data, the greatly increased scope did not impose a heavy cost. We recommend the use of a supplemental dataset of general organic chemistry to shape the latent space.
Specific bond types correlate strongly with the energetic stability of SEI candidate structures. P-F and Li-O bonds are associated with more stable structures. C-O and Li-F bonds are associated with less stable ones.  It will be possible to calculate properties such as Li+ diffusivity as a function of the starting formulation.

Data And Code Availability
The list of SEI candidate structures and energies can be found at the provided Figshare link. The original 1M LiPF6 in EC solution and plotting scripts are also available.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
We used a higher-priority dataset composed only of the periodic and cluster surface reaction subset. We applied decoupled weight norms with the norms not included in the optimizer. We found little effect of early stopping validation for this dataset.

Ethical Considerations
Content not peer-reviewed by ChemRxiv. License: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 4 shows bond counts with respect to total system energy for the most lithiated SEI candidate set. Table 1 contains the best available calculations for surface reaction energy barriers used for validation.

Three Takeaways
1. A multitask QRNN MLFF successfully ranks SEI candidates using enhanced sampling. 2. P-F and Li-O bonds correlate with stability, while C-O and Li-F do not. 3. General organic chemistry data expands latent space without harming battery task performance.
